extra.message: The `filter` argument of the `pastes` GraphQL query is interpolated with Python `%` string formatting directly into a raw SQL fragment passed to SQLAlchemy's `text()`. Any client can supply `filter` (e.g. `' UNION SELECT ...--`) to break out of the quoted literal and execute arbitrary SQL against the SQLite database, allowing extraction of the `users` table (including cleartext passwords).

`resolve_system_debug` concatenates the unvalidated GraphQL `arg` argument into the shell string `'ps {}'` and executes it via `helpers.run_cmd` -> `os.popen`. There is no authentication, no allowlist and no shell escaping, so `systemDebug(arg: "; id")` yields arbitrary OS command execution as the application user.

`resolve_system_diagnostics` passes the client-supplied `cmd` argument straight to `helpers.run_cmd` (`os.popen`). The only guard is `security.allowed_cmds`, which returns True unconditionally in the default (easy) server mode (core/security.py:33-39), and even in hard mode only checks a `startswith` prefix, so `cmd="echo x; id"` still executes. This is arbitrary command execution.

The `importPaste` mutation builds a shell command `curl --insecure {url}` from the attacker-controlled `scheme`, `host`, `port` and `path` arguments and runs it through `os.popen`. `security.strip_dangerous_characters` returns the string unchanged in the default easy mode and only strips `;` and `&` in hard mode (core/security.py:41-46), leaving backticks, `$(...)`, `|` and newlines usable for command injection.

`importPaste` fetches a fully attacker-controlled URL (scheme, host, port and path) with `curl --insecure` and returns the response body to the caller. There is no host allowlist or internal-network blocklist, so an unauthenticated client can force the server to request internal services (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:5013/`, cloud metadata endpoints) and read the responses — a full read SSRF.

`run_cmd` executes its argument through `os.popen`, which runs the string in a shell. It is the shared sink for `systemDebug`, `systemDiagnostics`, `importPaste` and `systemHealth`, all of which pass request-controlled data. No argument list, quoting or escaping is used anywhere.

`save_file` concatenates the caller-supplied `filename` onto `WEB_UPLOADDIR` and opens it for writing with no canonicalisation (`os.path.realpath`), no confinement check and no `secure_filename` sanitisation. A filename such as `../../app.py` or `../../../../home/dvga/.bashrc` escapes the upload directory and overwrites arbitrary files with attacker-controlled content, which on this Flask app leads to remote code execution.

The `uploadPaste` mutation takes a raw `filename` argument from the GraphQL request and passes it unvalidated to `helpers.save_file`, which uses it to build the write path. The externally supplied name fully controls the destination file, with no allowlist, extension check or directory confinement, and the mutation requires no authentication.

extra.message: `get_identity` decodes the JWT with `options={"verify_signature": False, "verify_exp": False}`, so the token's signature and expiry are never checked. Any client can hand-craft an unsigned token with `{"identity": "admin"}` and be treated as that user by `resolve_me`, and expired tokens remain valid forever. This is a complete authentication bypass.

extra.message: `resolve_me` derives the acting user solely from the `token` argument via `get_identity`, which does not verify the signature. Because the resulting username is then used to look up and return the `User` record, an attacker submitting a forged token impersonates any account (e.g. `admin`) and reads its data without ever authenticating.

`UserObject.resolve_password` decides whether to reveal the stored password by reading `identity` out of the request's own JSON body (`info.context.json.get('identity')`). The client controls that value, so simply POSTing `{"query": "...", "identity": "admin"}` makes the resolver return every user's cleartext password. Authorization must be derived from server-side session/token state, never from request-supplied fields.

extra.message: The `before_request` hook lets any unauthenticated client globally switch the server's security posture with the `X-DVGA-MODE` request header. Sending `X-DVGA-MODE: Beginner` calls `set_mode('easy')`, which disables the depth, cost, operation-name, denylist and introspection middlewares for every user (they all early-return when `is_level_easy()`), and re-enables the command allowlist bypass. A security decision affecting all clients is taken from an untrusted request header.

extra.message: `WEB_DEBUG` defaults to `True` when the environment variable is unset, so a deployment that forgets to set `WEB_DEBUG` runs with debug behaviour enabled. Note also that `os.environ.get` returns strings, so even `WEB_DEBUG=False` evaluates truthy — the flag can never be turned off through configuration.

The `systemDebug` diagnostic field is registered in the production schema (line 274) and runs process-listing commands on the host for any unauthenticated caller. Debug/diagnostic functionality of this kind should not be reachable in a deployed application; here it also serves as a command-injection sink.

`SECRET_KEY` and `JWT_SECRET_KEY` are hardcoded to the literal string `'dvga'` in source. Because the JWT signing key is public knowledge, anyone can mint a validly signed access token for any identity (including `admin`), and the Flask session signing key is equally forgeable. Secrets must come from the environment or a secret store.

The database seeder creates the `admin` account with the hardcoded weak password `changeme` (via `random_password()`, line 48-50) and the `operator` account with `password123`. These credentials are committed to the repository and are guessable by any attacker.

The `User.password` column stores passwords as cleartext — `create_user` writes the raw value (line 17-22) and `Login` authenticates with `User.query.filter_by(username=username, password=password)` (core/views.py:234), a direct plaintext comparison. No hashing (bcrypt/argon2/PBKDF2) or salting is applied, so any read of the database or of the `password` GraphQL field discloses usable credentials.

extra.message: Changing the global server security mode via `/difficulty/<level>` (and via the `X-DVGA-MODE` header in `before_request`, line 468-475) produces no security audit record. Unlike the GraphQL resolvers, which all call `Audit.create_audit_entry`, these paths write no entry to the `audits` table and there is no Flask logger, `after_request` hook or other shared logging in the request path, so a state change that disables all query protections is untraceable. The WebSocket subscription handler interpolates `paste.title`, `paste.content`, `paste.owner.name`, `paste.ipAddr` and `paste.userAgent` into an HTML template literal that is then parsed and inserted into the DOM by jQuery (`$(pasteHTML).prependTo(...)`). None of these attacker-controlled values are escaped, so a paste created with a payload like `` in its title or content executes JavaScript in every viewer's browser — stored XSS. Note `userAgent` is taken straight from the request header (core/views.py:125), so the sink is also reachable via header injection.

`get_pastes()` builds the paste gallery markup by interpolating the unescaped `title`, `content`, `owner`, `ipAddr` and `userAgent` values returned from `/graphql` into a template literal passed to `$(...).append()`, which parses it as HTML. Stored paste content therefore executes as script in the browser of anyone visiting `/my_pastes` or `/public_pastes`.

The `systemUpdate` query calls `security.simulate_load`, which blocks in a `time.sleep(0.1)` loop for 200-500 iterations (20-50 seconds) per invocation (core/security.py:8-16). The cost middleware that would reject it is disabled in the default easy mode, and the field is unauthenticated, so a handful of concurrent requests exhaust the server's worker capacity — uncontrolled resource consumption.

The `/graphql` endpoint is registered with `batch=True` and no limit on the number of operations per batch, no query complexity/cost cap in the default mode, and no rate limiting. A single request containing thousands of array-batched queries (or aliased/duplicated fields) multiplies server work arbitrarily, and also defeats any per-request throttling.

extra.message: `sys.setrecursionlimit(100000)` raises Python's stack-depth guard by three orders of magnitude specifically so that deeply nested GraphQL queries are parsed instead of rejected. Combined with the depth-check middleware being inactive in the default easy mode, a deeply recursive or circular-fragment query consumes memory and stack until the process crashes.

`resp.set_cookie("env", "graphiql:disable")` sets a cookie that is used for an access-control decision (core/middleware.py:122) without `httponly=True`, `secure=True` or `samesite`. The cookie is therefore readable and writable by client-side script and transmitted over plaintext HTTP.

extra.message: The interactive GraphiQL IDE is registered as a permanent route at `/graphiql` with `graphiql=True` and a verbose `format_error` handler. Its only gate is a client-editable cookie, so the full schema explorer and query console are effectively public — an information-disclosure and attack-surface misconfiguration for a deployed application.

`IntrospectionMiddleware` returns early whenever `is_level_easy()` — the default server state — so schema introspection (`__schema`) is fully available to unauthenticated clients. Even in hard mode the check only matches the field name `__schema` and misses `__type`, so introspection of individual types still succeeds. This discloses the complete API surface, including the administrative `deleteAllPastes`, `systemDebug` and `systemDiagnostics` fields.

extra.message: The `/graphql` endpoint accepts state-changing mutations (`createPaste`, `editPaste`, `deletePaste`, `uploadPaste`, `importPaste`) and destructive queries (`deleteAllPastes`, `readAndBurn`) with no CSRF token, no `SameSite` cookie policy and no Origin/Referer validation, and `OverriddenView.dispatch_request` additionally reads query parameters from `request.args` on GET requests. A cross-origin page can therefore trigger these operations on behalf of a visiting user.
